p2c1.essay:
Part One ended with a man falling onto a sofa. Part Two opens on the same sofa, and I think the most important fact about this chapter is arithmetical: the crime took one part of the book, and there are five still to come. Whatever Dostoevsky is interested in, it is mostly not the murder. Raskolnikov supplies the missing word himself within the first few pages, 'Surely it isn't my punishment coming upon me? It is!', and what he means by it is not the police. He means that he cannot think.

Remember what he believed in [[p1c6]]: that criminals are caught because reason and will desert them at the critical moment, like a disease, and that he would be exempt, because what he planned was 'not a crime'. The opening pages here are that theory being falsified in his own body, almost as a controlled experiment. He searches his clothes three times and forgets the pockets full of loot. He stuffs the trinkets into a hole that 'bulged out more than ever' and feels gleeful. He leaves the cut-off bloody fringe in the middle of the floor. He falls asleep holding the evidence in his fist. The fever is real, and the chills and chattering teeth keep it physical, but I don't think we are allowed to say the fever explains everything. The novel is careful to leave open which is cause and which is symptom.

Then the summons, and the walk to the station through the same heat and stench as the book's first page. Twice on the way he decides to confess: 'perhaps I'll simply tell', then 'fall on my knees, and confess everything'. This is the morning after. I find that astonishing every time, and it changes how I read what follows: the suspense of this novel is not only whether he will be caught. It is what he will do with an urge he already has.

The police office is one of Dostoevsky's great comic rooms, and it is worth noticing that it is comic. A vain lieutenant with a horizontal moustache, a pomaded clerk with rings, a German madam in a dress like 'an air-balloon' telling a story about an author who played the piano with his foot. Raskolnikov walks in expecting the tragic climax of his life and finds a farce about a landlady's unpaid bill. The relief makes him giddy, and giddiness makes him reckless: he ticks off the lieutenant for smoking, enjoys it, then pours out his whole history, the dead girl he was to marry, the I O U, to officials who keep telling him it is not their business. Watch what he is doing. He is trying out the part of an ordinary wronged young man, somebody with a story other people could sympathise with.

And then comes the paragraph the chapter exists for. In the middle of his performance something shuts. He feels 'everlasting solitude and remoteness', feels that even if these were his own brothers and sisters it would be out of the question to appeal to them about anything, ever. Dostoevsky insists it is 'more a sensation than a conception or idea', and the phrasing matters. Raskolnikov is a man who lives by ideas; an idea was all he had in Part One. The first real consequence of the deed arrives as something below thought, a bodily knowledge that he has stepped outside the circle of people one can speak to. Nobody has accused him. Nobody in the room suspects him. The sentence has been passed anyway, and he would hardly have heard a burning at the stake over the noise of it. If I had to point to one passage that explains the second word of the title, it would be this one, and there is no courtroom in sight.

The ending turns the screw with wonderful economy. He stands up to confess to the kindly superintendent, and at that exact moment overhears the two officers arguing about the case: Koch, Pestryakov, the door that was bolted and then was not. For anyone who has just read [[p1c7]] it is dizzying. We stood behind that door with him, and here is the view from the landing, more or less correctly reasoned out. He faints. And the tone of the room changes. Ilya Petrovitch's questions, 'Did you go out yesterday?', 'At what time?', are short and no longer silly, and Nikodim Fomitch's protest dies under the head clerk's stare. Two tiny sentences follow, and the farce is over. Whether the officers really suspect anything, or whether a sick student has only frightened himself, the chapter does not say. Raskolnikov is sure. That may be the more dangerous fact.

annotations.quote: Surely it isn’t beginning already! Surely it isn’t my punishment coming upon me? It is!
annotations.note: The second word of the title, spoken by the criminal himself a few hours after the crime, and it refers to nothing any court could impose. What frightens him is that his memory and reasoning are failing. In [[p1c6]] he had decided that this was exactly what would not happen to him.

annotations.quote: So he had been asleep with them in his hand.
annotations.note: The bloody sock, the fringe and the pocket lining, clutched like a child's toy while the porter and Nastasya stand over him. Nastasya even jokes that he sleeps with his rags like a treasure. Dostoevsky gets a great deal of dread out of people almost noticing.

annotations.quote: He was flinging himself on his knees to pray, but broke into laughter--not at the idea of prayer, but at himself.
annotations.note: A very exact sentence. The narrator will not let us think Raskolnikov is a scoffer; the instinct to pray is still there and he does not despise it. What he finds ridiculous is himself, of all people, asking.

annotations.quote: That’s all conventional, that’s all relative, merely a way of looking at it
annotations.note: The philosophy of Part One, applied to a sock soaked in blood. He can tell himself that disgust is only a convention, and the narrator adds that the thought runs 'only on the top surface of his mind' while the rest of him shudders. The whole chapter is that split between what the head says and what the body knows.

annotations.quote: a sickening smell of fresh paint and stale oil from the newly decorated rooms
annotations.note: Easy to pass as atmosphere, but he has smelt fresh paint very recently: the empty flat he hid in on the way down the pawnbroker's stairs in [[p1c7]] was being painted. I would keep that smell in mind when he reaches for his hat at the end of the chapter.

annotations.quote: To his own surprise he, too, grew suddenly angry and found a certain pleasure in it.
annotations.note: Relief coming out as insolence. A minute ago he thought he was walking to his arrest; now he is lecturing a police lieutenant about cigarettes. It is the worst possible moment to make himself memorable, and he cannot resist it.

annotations.quote: Poverty is not a vice, my friend, but we know you go off like powder
annotations.note: The same proverb Marmeladov opened with in the tavern in [[p1c2]], now in the mouth of a good-natured policeman. Garnett's 'Explosive Lieutenant' a line later renders a nickname that in Russian is simply Lieutenant Gunpowder, which is why the superintendent keeps playing on powder and firing up.

annotations.quote: A gloomy sensation of agonising, everlasting solitude and remoteness, took conscious form in his soul.
annotations.note: I think this is the centre of the chapter. It comes straight after his attempt to win the room's sympathy, and it is described as a physical sensation, not a thought. He has not been found out by anyone, and he is already cut off from everyone.

annotations.quote: No, better cast off the burden without thinking.
annotations.note: He is on his feet and one sentence from confessing, less than a day after the crime. Notice that he distrusts thinking here: thinking is what got him into this. What stops him is not a change of mind but an overheard conversation.

annotations.quote: There was a sudden silence. It was strange.
annotations.note: Seven words that change the temperature of the room. Up to now the officers have been comic types; now three of them exchange looks over a fainting student who went out 'about seven' the evening before. The chapter leaves it at a silence and lets him, and us, fill it in.

links.why: His confident theory of why other criminals lose their heads, and why he would not, sits right beside this morning of forgotten pockets and rags on the floor.
The officers' argument about Koch, Pestryakov and the bolted door is the same few minutes we lived through from the other side of the door.
Marmeladov's 'poverty is not a vice' returns here from a policeman, and the tavern confession makes an instructive pair with Raskolnikov's own outpouring to strangers.
The pomaded head clerk with the rings is worth remembering; he gets a scene of his own.

p2c2.essay:
This chapter is a walk, six hours of it, and it has the logic of a walk taken in a fever: each plan is replaced by the next before it can be carried out. The canal, then the Neva, then the Islands, then a yard he happens to pass. I like how unheroic the concealment is. The things for which two women died go under a stone beside a workmen's convenience (Garnett's 'sink', and the chalked joke about standing, are being polite about what the place is), and the whole business takes a minute. He feels again what he felt in the police office, 'an intense, almost unbearable joy', and laughs his thin noiseless laugh all the way across the square.

It lasts until the boulevard where, in [[p1c4]], he tried to rescue a drunk girl and gave a policeman twenty copecks. Hold on to that sum. Then comes the real event of the chapter, which is a question: if he did this deliberately, for a definite object, how is it that he never even looked inside the purse? He was about to drop it in the water uncounted. The arithmetic he overheard in the tavern in [[p1c6]], one death weighed against a hundred lives and the old woman's money put to good use, evaporates in a sentence, and what I admire is that Dostoevsky does not let him be surprised. 'He had known it all before.' He knew at the box, with his hands in it. So the money was never the reason, and the chapter declines to say what was. He declines too: 'It is because I am very ill.' I would rather leave that question open here than suggest answers; the book has not finished asking it.

What fills the gap is hatred, 'almost physical', of every face in the street, and then his feet bring him to Razumihin's door. He had promised himself in [[p1c5]] to go 'the day after', and here he is, on schedule and not by choice. This is our first sight of Razumihin, and he is all there at once: ragged, unshaven, talking a streak about hack translation, generous without making a ceremony of it. He splits his advance with a man who has just insulted him and passes it off as self-interest. The pamphlet he is translating, 'Is woman a human being?', is Dostoevsky's joke at the expense of advanced publishing, but in this book the joke has an edge. Raskolnikov has just acted on the proposition that a certain old woman was not quite one.

He takes the three roubles, then climbs the stairs again to give them back. It is easy to read that as delirium. I think it is consistent. In the police office he found he could no longer appeal to anyone; here he finds he can no longer accept from anyone. Work, wages, a friend's help: these are the ordinary ways a poor student gets by, the ways he had judged too slow. Now they are held out to him, and he cannot bear to touch them.

Then the bridge, which is the passage I would reread. A coachman's whip comes down across his back, and it is hard not to hear the dream of [[p1c5]] in it, except that he is now on the receiving end, and the bystanders laugh as they laughed there. A woman, sorry for the blow, presses twenty copecks on him 'in Christ's name'. The coin he once gave away comes back to him as alms; he has changed sides of the transaction. And he turns to the famous view, the cathedral dome and the palace across water that is, for once, blue. We are told this panorama always left him 'strangely cold'. Garnett's 'blank and lifeless' is tamer than the Russian, which says the splendid picture was full of a spirit deaf and dumb. What strikes him now is that he has stopped at his old spot as though he could still think his old thoughts. He cannot. His whole past seems to lie somewhere far beneath his feet, and he has the sensation of flying upward away from it, which ought to feel like freedom and plainly does not.

So he throws the coin into the river. Of everything he does in these two chapters, burying the purse included, that small gesture seems to me the most final. The purse he hid from the police. The coin he refuses from humankind, and the narrator says as much: he had 'cut himself off from everyone and from everything at that moment.' He himself did the cutting, with a sweep of the arm, in sunlight, a day and a half after the axe.

The coda is a nightmare he takes for fact, the lieutenant from the police office beating the landlady on the stairs, and Nastasya's diagnosis, 'It's the blood', which is folk medicine and lands on him like an accusation.

annotations.quote: And what if the boxes were to float instead of sinking? And of course they would.
annotations.note: The planner of Part One is gone. He decided on the canal in delirium and only now, standing over the water, thinks about whether jewel-cases sink. The dry 'of course they would' sounds to me like the narrator shaking his head.

annotations.quote: on the hoarding above had been scribbled in chalk the time-honoured witticism
annotations.note: The sign forbids 'standing', and Garnett leaves the reader to work out what men stand there to do; her 'sink' is the yard's urinal trough. So the proceeds of the great experiment end up in the least dignified corner of Petersburg, chosen because nobody would wonder at a man slipping in.

annotations.quote: It has been lying there most likely ever since the house was built, and will lie as many years more.
annotations.note: He trusts the stone the way he could not trust the hole in his wallpaper. Notice that he has not counted, opened or even looked properly at what he is burying. That fact catches up with him about two hundred yards later.

annotations.quote: how is it I did not even glance into the purse and don’t know what I had there
annotations.note: The most damaging question anyone asks in the book so far, and he asks it of himself. If the motive was money for a fresh start, an uncounted purse under a stone makes no sense. He answers by blaming illness, which is not an answer.

annotations.quote: because you are kinder than anyone--cleverer, I mean, and can judge
annotations.note: He says 'kinder' and corrects it at once to 'cleverer'. Kindness is what he came for and what he cannot stand to be seen wanting. The slip tells more truth than the rest of the speech.

annotations.quote: Heruvimov is going to bring out this work as a contribution to the woman question
annotations.note: The 'woman question' was a live cause in the Russian press of the 1860s, and Dostoevsky is teasing the publishers who cashed in on it with padded German pamphlets. Razumihin knows it is charlatanism and translates it anyway, cheerfully, for six roubles a sheet. That is one way of being poor; Raskolnikov chose another.

annotations.quote: Take it, my good man, in Christ’s name.
annotations.note: He is taken for a beggar, and given exactly twenty copecks, the sum he handed a policeman for a stranger's sake in [[p1c4]]. The phrase is the ordinary Russian formula for alms, but it is still the first time anyone has spoken that name to him since the crime.

annotations.quote: It left him strangely cold; this gorgeous picture was for him blank and lifeless.
annotations.note: The view is of official Petersburg at its grandest, palace and cathedral, and even as a student he felt nothing in it for him. Dostoevsky's Russian is stranger than Garnett's: the picture is filled with a 'deaf and dumb spirit'. He never did explain the feeling to himself, and the chapter does not explain it either.

annotations.quote: with a sweep of his arm flung it into the water; then he turned and went home
annotations.note: He could not throw the stolen things in the water, and this he throws without hesitation. A stranger's charity turns out to be harder to carry than the pawnbroker's purse.

annotations.quote: That’s the blood crying in your ears.
annotations.note: Nastasya means it medically: blood with no outlet clots and makes you hear things. But she has just said 'It's the blood' to a man who turned white at the word. Garnett's 'crying' is a lucky choice, with its faint echo of blood that cries out.

links.why: The girl on the boulevard, the whiskered policeman and the first twenty copecks: the bench he cannot bear to pass now.
Where he resolved to visit Razumihin 'the day after', and where the whip and the laughing crowd first appeared, in a dream.
The overheard case for killing the old woman rested on what her money could do; set it beside the purse he never opens.
The joy at the stone repeats the joy in the police office, and the solitude on the bridge completes what began there.

p2c3.essay:
After two chapters locked inside one overheated skull, the door opens and Razumihin has to stoop to get through it. The change of air is so complete that it is almost a change of genre. There is soup, a clean cloth, 'real pillows', beer sent up by a landlady who a few days ago was suing him; there is a messenger who says 'your mamma' and a friend who teases him for it. I find it one of the warmest chapters in the book so far, and I think the warmth is the point, because Raskolnikov experiences every bit of it as a threat.

Look at what Razumihin has done in four days. He found the address through the bureau in two minutes, charmed the landlady, bought back the I O U for ten roubles, fetched a doctor, and made friends with the whole cast of the police office from [[p2c1]]. From the sofa, each kindness is a breach in the wall. His name is on a register. His friend sees the head clerk almost daily. That same Zametov has stood in this room, hunted for a sock, and handed it to him. In Razumihin's mouth the detail is comedy, and it is comedy, and it is also the worst thing Raskolnikov could hear. The whole chapter runs on that double register: one man narrating a jolly rescue, the other listening for the sentence that will mean he is finished. 'What did I rave about?' he asks, and asks again.

So he does something new. He decides to lie low, out of 'almost animal' cunning, and lets himself be spoon-fed when he could sit up. The theorist of Part One has become a creature in a burrow. The moment he is alone he is out of bed checking the hole, the stove, the sock, planning a flight to America, and then half a bottle of cold beer puts him to sleep like a child. It is very funny and rather pitiful.

The second half belongs to the bundle of clothes, Razumihin's best comic turn, with its price-list and its embassy secretary's boots. But follow the money. The thirty-five roubles come from his mother, the remittance promised in her letter in [[p1c3]], squeezed out of a pension. At first he refuses to sign for it. At the end he asks what paid for the clothes, and the answer is: she did. He has been dressed from head to foot by exactly the kind of sacrifice he could not bear to accept, and his one private thought about the people doing all this for him is 'It will be long before I get rid of them.'

annotations.quote: he felt that he had forgotten something he ought to remember
annotations.note: The delirium is written from inside and it is cunningly done. Everything is there, the crowd, the plotting, the fear, except the one fact, which Garnett sets in italics as a bare 'that'. His mind protects him from the memory and torments him with its absence at once.

annotations.quote: not Razumihin, as I am always called, but Vrazumihin, a student and gentleman
annotations.note: A joke that needs a gloss. 'Razum' is Russian for reason or good sense, and 'vrazumit' means to knock sense into someone. He is announcing his job in this novel while introducing himself to a messenger.

annotations.quote: For just now, brother, money is sweeter to us than treacle.
annotations.note: Razumihin's attitude to money in one line: it is something you need, so you take it and say thank you. Raskolnikov's next words are 'I don't want it.' He will not put his name to his mother's roubles until Razumihin threatens to guide his hand.

annotations.quote: as clumsily as a bear put his left arm round Raskolnikov’s head
annotations.note: He blows on soup that is 'only just warm'. I love that touch; the tenderness is real and slightly ridiculous. And the man being cradled is watching him 'wildly', full of alarm, calculating.

annotations.quote: from some queer, almost animal, cunning he conceived the idea of hiding his strength
annotations.note: A new mode for him. He is not reasoning here, he is hiding, the way a hunted thing goes still. Garnett's 'queer' is doing honest work: the narrator himself seems unsure where the impulse comes from.

annotations.quote: in two minutes they looked you up! Your name is down there.
annotations.note: Razumihin offers this as a funny story about bureaucracy. Raskolnikov's reply is two words, 'My name!' To a man who believes he has buried his tracks, the discovery that the city can produce him in two minutes is not funny at all.

annotations.quote: It was base of me to say that.... My mother herself is almost a beggar
annotations.note: Said 'loudly and distinctly', the one thing he volunteers in the whole chapter. He confesses a small lie about his mother's money with a kind of ferocity. I hear in it the pressure of the confession he is not making.

annotations.quote: with his own scented, ring-bedecked fingers he gave you the rag
annotations.note: The head clerk of the police office has held the sock from [[p2c1|the morning after]] in his hand and given it back. Razumihin is telling an anecdote about a dandy; the listener is working out whether he is already lost. The rings are the same ones Raskolnikov stared at while waiting his turn.

annotations.quote: Well, now let us pass to the United States of America, as they called them at school.
annotations.note: A schoolboy pun that cannot cross into English: 'shtaty', States, sounds like 'shtany', trousers. Garnett translates it straight and lets it sit there, puzzling. It lands oddly beside Raskolnikov's own thought, a few pages back, of escaping to America.

annotations.quote: What money was all that bought with?
annotations.note: The only thing he asks about his new clothes. Razumihin has given prices to the copeck and thinks the question is forgetfulness. It is the reverse: he has remembered whose money it is.

links.why: His mother's letter promised this remittance through Vahrushin, and told him what it cost her to raise it.
The sock, the fringe, the I O U and Zametov's rings all come back here, retold as a comic story by someone who does not know what they mean.
The friend he walked out on without giving an address is the one who has spent four days finding and nursing him.

p2c4.essay:
A murderer lies on a sofa with his face to the wall while two acquaintances discuss, across his body, who committed his murder. That is the whole staging of this chapter, and Dostoevsky gets from it something an ordinary detective story cannot: we already hold the answer, so every step of Razumihin's reconstruction can be marked against [[p1c7]]. He gets full marks. The murderer was behind the bolted door when Koch knocked; he slipped out when Koch went for the porter; he hid in the empty flat the painters had just run out of; the ear-rings fell from his pocket there. That last item is news even to Raskolnikov, which is why his one outburst, 'Behind the door?', comes with 'a blank look of terror'. He is hearing for the first time about something he left behind.

What interests me more than the accuracy is the method. Razumihin argues from character. Two painters who were rolling about in the gateway 'like children', thumping each other and laughing in front of a dozen witnesses, cannot have axed two women five minutes before: the mood does not fit the act. The police prefer the jewel-case and the attempted hanging, and put the wonderful, damning question about how an innocent man could be frightened. Facts against psychology: the argument is announced here in so many words, and it is worth keeping an ear open for it. So is a name dropped in passing among the party guests, Porfiry Petrovitch, head of the Investigation Department and Razumihin's distant relation.

Then there is Nikolay, whom it is easy to treat as a piece of plot. A frightened peasant pawns the cross off his neck for a drink and tries to hang himself, by his own account not from guilt but 'from anxiety' that he would be accused. An innocent man is in a cell for what the man on the sofa did. Nobody in the room can know that, and the one who does says nothing.

His silence is the other half of the chapter. Nastasya, who has no theory at all, does what the clever men do not. She blurts out that Lizaveta was murdered too, and adds that Lizaveta once mended a shirt for him. He turns to the wallpaper and counts the petals on a flower. The men talk on about 'the old pawnbroker-woman' and he lies still; it is the sister's name that takes the feeling out of his arms and legs.

Zossimov's verdict on the true account closes the scene: 'too melodramatic'. I take that as Dostoevsky smiling at his own plot. The truth has been spoken aloud in the murderer's room and dismissed for fitting too well.

annotations.quote: All his acquaintances found him tedious, but said he was clever at his work.
annotations.note: Dostoevsky's portraits often end with a sting like this. Zossimov is spick and span, loose-coated, ringed, and a bore. Set him against Razumihin in rags: the chapter is partly a contest between a man of correct opinions and a man of warm ones.

annotations.quote: Porfiry Petrovitch, the head of the Investigation Department here... But you know him.
annotations.note: Tossed off in a list of party guests, between an old uncle and a musician. Make a note of the name. Razumihin's circle of friends, it turns out, is drawn rather close around this case.

annotations.quote: She used to come here. She mended a shirt for you, too.
annotations.note: Until now Lizaveta has been a figure in a market and then a face in a doorway. Nastasya puts her inside this house with his shirt in her hands. No one else in the room attaches any importance to the remark.

annotations.quote: He did not attempt to move, but stared obstinately at the flower.
annotations.note: Petals, scallops, lines: he counts the wallpaper to keep from hearing. It is the most that Dostoevsky shows of his reaction, and it is enough. The body answers first again, limbs 'lifeless as though they had been cut off', as it did in the police office in [[p2c1]].

annotations.quote: lying is a delightful thing, for it leads to truth
annotations.note: Razumihin at his most characteristic, and I think he half means it: people who blunder and bluster get somewhere, people who worship their own blunders do not. He says it to a room containing one man who is lying by keeping silent, which he cannot know.

annotations.quote: But facts are not everything--at least half the business lies in how you interpret them!
annotations.note: A statement of method, and a good one. The jewel-case is a fact; what it proves depends on whether you ask who Nikolay is. It works as a hint about how to read this novel too, where we were given every fact of the crime in Part One and still cannot say why it happened.

annotations.quote: How could you be frightened, if you felt free from guilt?
annotations.note: The question that enrages Razumihin, and rightly: only someone who has never been poor and questioned by the police could ask it. It carries a second charge for the listener on the sofa, who has spent three chapters discovering how fear and guilt actually behave.

annotations.quote: Behind the door? Lying behind the door? Behind the door?
annotations.note: The only words he volunteers during the whole account, three times over. We were behind that door with him in [[p1c7]] and did not see the box fall either. Razumihin thinks he has woken from a dream; watch Zossimov, who 'slightly shook his head'.

annotations.quote: do their state of mind, their squeals and giggles and childish scuffling at the gate fit in with axes, bloodshed, fiendish cunning, robbery?
annotations.note: The defence from psychology. Men who have just killed do not roll about laughing in a gateway. It is persuasive, and it invites the question of what a man who has just killed does look like. We have had three chapters of the answer.

annotations.quote: Why, because everything fits too well... it’s too melodramatic.
annotations.note: The correct solution, rejected on grounds of taste. I enjoy the nerve of it: Dostoevsky has a character complain that the events of [[p1c7]] are implausible fiction. In this book the truth has trouble being believed.

links.why: Razumihin's reconstruction can be checked line by line against what happened on the staircase, including the empty flat with the open door.
The officers' first argument about Koch and Pestryakov, and the faint that Razumihin mentions so innocently here.
The tavern talk in which Lizaveta is described at length, meek and put-upon, long before Nastasya brings her into his room by name.
The investigator named in passing here appears in person.
